articles.title: Lil Finder Guy pet was the gateway to building my own Mac apps with Codex
articles.subtitle: At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet. This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it?
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet.

This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it? My first real task with Codex was putting together a virtual Lil Finder Guy for fun.

A month later, I’m using two Mac apps that Codex built at my direction. Toying around with Codex Pets was the gateway for me to better understand its capabilities.

OpenAI tools for making apps have improved a lot since last summer

Both Mac apps are just for my use and not intended for distribution, but that’s just a choice and not a Codex limitation. They’re genuinely usable and useful software applications that serve my needs.

One tool is called Flow, and it just helps me track activity and changes around the App Store. Another offers a better experience with using a social network on the Mac without certain constraints of Chrome, like minimum window width.

The experience taught me just how much these tools have changed since this time last year as well.

For example, I wanted to make my own Launchpad replacement when macOS Tahoe removed the feature from the Mac last June. (Launchpad wasn’t for everyone, but it was part of my muscle memory since OS X Lion. I’ve since moved on from missing it.)

Using ChatGPT to walk me through Xcode while copying and pasting blocks of code and screenshots of errors was a process void of much joy. Even as a proof-of-concept, I couldn’t get the app that I was making to resemble the behavior that I had in mind. Nuking the project felt good.

With Codex, I had a functioning app that solved my specific need in almost no time (and literally no Xcode). I was able to go from idea to minimum viable software almost immediately. The rest of my first month with Codex and making the app was spent adding features beyond my original need and getting more specific about how things should look and behave.

There are more tools that I want to make for myself next, and having Codex’s capabilities on the Mac has been a real boost.

(Next, I’ll be watching Apple’s WWDC announcements with a new eye for what additional capabilities become available. I’m also cautious about any changes that may break my newfound system for turning ideas into functioning tools.)

Computer Use in Codex is a major unlock

Part of what makes Codex good at this compared to my experience using ChatGPT a year ago is that the model and app are made for coding and generally just doing things for you.

ChatGPT will absorb most or all of this functionality as a feature within the main app, but the extent of this remains to be seen. For now, there’s one thing in particular about Codex that made all the difference in the world: Computer Use.

Codex is far from the only coding agent available on the Mac, and it’s not the only version with a computer use feature either. But Codex’s Computer Use feature is phenomenal. On the Mac, it works in the background without taking over your machine. For me, this has meant I’ve been able to use my Mac, uninterrupted, while this coding agent expertly follows my direction.

Codex’s Computer Use essentially unlocks the complete opposite experience from what ChatGPT provided in this department last summer. Instead of it providing me with guidance and not much perspective, I’ve been able to guide it and vastly expand my own perspective.

You don’t have to spend a lot to get Codex experience

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

articles.title: Splatoon Raiders review: Nintendo's take on Borderlands is a delightful mess
articles.subtitle: The Switch 2 exclusive is a full-blown looter shooter that goes way deeper than you'd expect Usually when the word “mess” appears in a video game review, it’s a bad sign. Splatoon Raiders is an exception to the rule.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
The Switch 2 exclusive is a full-blown looter shooter that goes way deeper than you'd expect

Usually when the word “mess” appears in a video game review, it’s a bad sign. Splatoon Raiders is an exception to the rule. The ink-splattered Nintendo Switch 2 shooter is a mess in the most positive sense of the word. In its most pulse-pounding moments, when I’m trying to ink my way out of a Salmonid mosh pit that overtakes the screen, I feel like a kid tossing mashed potato bombs in the center of a cafeteria food fight. The sloppier the battlefield gets, the wider my devilish grin becomes.

That experience isn’t unique to Splatoon Raiders. It’s something that has drawn me to Nintendo’s multiplayer-forward Splatoon series since its Wii U debut. The simple delight of drenching arenas in colorful ink still hasn’t failed to charm me after over a decade of shootouts.

As a single-player spin-off that cranks the spirit of childhood mayhem up even further, the delightfully untidy Splatoon Raiders has finally helped me pin down the series’ lasting appeal. Sometimes it’s cathartic to make a big mess that no one can tell you to clean up. Make me, loser!

Built as a single-player adventure with co-op support, Splatoon Raiders puts you in control of an Inkling dubbed The Mechanic.

After getting caught up in a freak storm with Deep Cut, the Splatoon universe’s best pop band, you’re left stranded in the Spirhalite Islands, a series of landmasses inhabited by the same angry Salmonids that terrorize Splatoon 3 ’s Salmon Run mode — googly-eyed fish, steel snakes, mechanical dolphins, etc.

That misfortune presents an opportunity: The islands are filled with valuable treasures, so you decide to set up shop rather than look for an escape. Splatoon’s wacky lore gets put to good use in collectible scrolls that tease out an economic crisis plaguing Splatsville. (And you know what happens when an Inkling goes underwater. )

The story itself is mostly just there to motivate a fun treasure hunting campaign. As The Mechanic, you’ll fight through a series of compact levels with a bot buddy that can help you take down enemy mobs while looking for loot and crafting materials. You can see shades of various Splatoon modes from the series’ past in that structure.

Some stages have you fighting through linear levels with shooting and light platforming that wouldn’t feel out of place in Splatoon 3 ’s solo campaign. Others toss you into arenas where you need to splat waves of Salmonids and collect Power Eggs, adapting the winning PvE structure of Salmon Run to something more solo-friendly.

Other challenge levels, which give you a specific loadout or toss you into a combat gauntlet centered around one enemy type, feel right out of Splatoon 2 ’s excellent Octo Expansion DLC. The series’ history of experimentation pays off in a single-player game that mashes several great ideas into one splattershot collage that’s still cohesive as a standalone spin-off.

All the fundamentals of Splatoon remain intact. You’re still shooting at enemies with the inky weapons you’d use in a multiplayer turf war. The terrain gets covered in blots that you can swim in to refill your ammo and evade enemies, a clever mix of action and traversal that’s still novel after all these years. Most of it cleanly translates to a single-player adventure, though not quite everything.

Some weapon classes that were built for team dynamics, like Rollers and Chargers, feel ill-equipped to manage denser packs of Salmonids on their own. What’s more, only being able to keep one weapon equipped at a time feels like a restriction born from the core series that doesn’t suit a new breed of game.

And that game is a loud-and-proud looter shooter. Splatoon Raiders ’ closest parallels are, surprisingly, Borderlands and Diablo: It’s a full-on action RPG where you grab piles of weapons with increasing levels, stats, and perks. Steady progression is the name of the game, as you boost your stats alongside your weapons and gradually turn a weak Inkling with a pea shooter into a one-squid wrecking machine.

That means that the early hours of Splatoon Raiders can feel a little simple as you complete light, short challenges featuring a familiar cast of enemies that have barely been tweaked for a different style of game. But the chaos and challenge creep up on you throughout the 15-hour story and beyond.

The key to that success is in Splatoon Raiders ’ approach to character builds, which turns the series into a more kid-friendly Outriders with a few tweaks. The Mechanic can equip one of three ink tanks at a time, each one giving them access to an array of secondary weapons that operate on cooldowns.

The Tactical Tank grants access to a turret and a wind turbine, among other gadgets, while the Power Tank gets a ground-pounding fist, a spinning top of doom, and more. The early game fun comes from crafting each gadget, testing them out, and figuring out a combination that best complements your playstyle.

Splatoon Raiders is the most kid-friendly rage room in town.

Like any good ARPG, everything picks up once you start locking in decisions and get into nitty-gritty tinkering. Each gadget can be augmented with perks that make it more devastating as your power levels grow. Take the Splattelites, a rotating ring of damaging ink blots that you can summon around you for a spell.

On the Mac? It’s been a different story since the Touch Bar was discontinued.

articles.title: Building on Burnout and an underwhelming predecessor are Wreckreation 2’s missions, and so far it’s a promising patch of Paradise
articles.subtitle: Principles vs player expression "Wreckreation wasn’t actually an attempt to recreate Burnout," former Criterion Games studio head Fiona Sperry says as she and her team reveal their latest arcade racer, Wreckreation 2. "I think some people thought it was.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Principles vs player expression

"Wreckreation wasn’t actually an attempt to recreate Burnout," former Criterion Games studio head Fiona Sperry says as she and her team reveal their latest arcade racer, Wreckreation 2. "I think some people thought it was.

But it was actually an exploration of freedom and creativity in racing games, and that was really a continuation of unfinished work at the end of [Burnout] Paradise and also the game we were making before we left EA. It was really about asking the question, ‘What if we gave players an enormous amount of freedom? ’"

Whatever the intention, the blend of Burnout-ish arcade racing and player-built, GTA Online-esque airborne tracks that Sperry and studio Three Fields Entertainment put out last year didn’t stick the landing after launching off the release mega-ramp.

Since she and some colleagues left EA-owned Criterion in 2014, their efforts have been defined in a lot of folks' minds - mine included - largely in terms of what they used to do. After Paradise, EA binned the widely beloved and successful Burnout series Sperry and co forged their reputations in, moving Criterion on to Need For Speed.

Today, the studio are just one of many working on the corp’s monolithic Battlefield shooters.

Thus, whether fair or not, it’s hard to look at any new game from the likes of Three Fields or the equally ex-Criteriony Fuse Games - the latter being the developers of Star Wars: Galactic Racer - without hunting around for evidence it’s bringing back the rush of slamming a Hunter Cavalry into a wall from behind the wheel of a Carson Inferno Van.

This, I’m sure, is both a blessing and a curse for the devs in question, but ironically I think that despite Sperry’s pushback against the idea that Wreckreation was about recapturing Burnout, its freshly announced sequel Wreckreation 2 might be the closest her studio have come yet to achieving that.

Built as a clear reaction to the shortcomings of their last game, by a Three Fields team reborn under the new name When Tides Turn, Wreckreation 2’s designed to be more focused and physical than its unwieldy and awkwardly bouncy predecessor.

A vast expanse that’s fairly bland and empty outside of some switchbacked roads has been ditched in favour of map set in and around Heartbreak City, an Eastern US-esque metropolis whose name possibly betrays how its creators were feeling when they set about picking up the pieces following their last game’s release.

The driving model’s designed so that cars can much more naturally bump, bash, and grind against each other. Booting up an early build that I’ve been able to whip around after learning about the game for the first time, things instantly felt much closer to Burnout Paradise than any game this set of devs have built since exiting Criterion all those years ago.

Fair enough, I’ve only been able to try a dozen or so events in a limited section of Heartbreak City, with When Tides Turn still at an early stage of development.

All of the events will be familiar to any Burnout fan - traditional races, one-on-one face-offs, the classic road rages in which wrecking as many opponents as possible is the key, and wreckonings, that being the name adopted for time trials that reward a faster version of the same car.

Speaking of cars, this first demo had two - the quick Dearborn & Schaeffer Nightranger hypercar and a brawny 50s muscle car called the Huntsville Nebraska. Rather than a single base version and one special variant you earn by winning its wreckoning, as was the case in Paradise, each of the rides in Wreckreation 2 so far come with two special variants, with each bringing a visual overhaul and step up in performance.

According to Sperry, Wreckreation 2’s been in the works for "about three months" at this point, with only eight weeks of that coming after the studio moved away from supporting the first Wreckreation on a full-time basis. Given that, what they’ve built thus far has largely impressed me.

A city with building-lined avenues and narrow alleyways makes for a much more natural setting for road rages in particular than open alpine roads with little scenery. The car collisions are nowhere near as stilted as in the first game, even if the vehicles still feel like they’re lacking a bit of weight on a controller.

The drifting’s serviceable, especially when behind the wheel of the rapid Nightranger, if not as seamlessly satisfying as it was in Paradise and its predecessors.

Though, it’s still plain to see at this point that Wreckreation 2 has a long way to go. At least this time that’s an explicit part of the devs’ plan. In their new guise, the team plan to be a lot more open throughout their development process, seeking rounds of player feedback long before the full version releases.

articles.title: The Real System Requirements for OS 27
articles.subtitle: Apple has released public betas of macOS 27 Golden Gate, iOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and tvOS 27, along with a developer beta of visionOS 27 (see “ Apple Opens Public Betas for OS 27,” 20 July 2026). We expect final releases in September or October.
articles.author: TidBITS
articles.content:
Apple has released public betas of macOS 27 Golden Gate, iOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and tvOS 27, along with a developer beta of visionOS 27 (see “ Apple Opens Public Betas for OS 27,” 20 July 2026). We expect final releases in September or October. Many people are eager to learn whether their current hardware will support the new operating systems or if they’ll need to consider upgrading to stay current.

This year marks a significant shift: Apple has dropped all Intel-based Macs, completing its transition to Apple silicon across the Mac lineup. iPadOS 27 and watchOS 27 each drop five models, but iOS 27 will run on the same models as iOS 26.

Apple Intelligence Requirements

The primary software requirement that remains is Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16 models, iPad mini (A17 Pro), and iPad and Mac models equipped with an M-series chip, plus the A18 Pro-powered MacBook Neo. All watchOS 27-capable Apple Watch models are compatible with Apple Intelligence when paired with an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone. Several additional tiers have also emerged:

Customizable Siri expressivity: To customize the expressivity and pace of Siri’s voice, you’ll need an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, or iPhone Air; iPad models with M4 and later and at least 12 GB of unified memory, Mac models with M3 and later and at least 12 GB of unified memory; or the M5 version of the Apple Vision Pro.

Improved Dictation accuracy: This on-device model requires an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, or iPhone Air; iPad models with M4 and later and at least 12 GB of unified memory; and Mac models with M3 and later and at least 12 GB of unified memory.

Determining precisely which features rely on Apple Intelligence is becoming difficult, but if you want Apple Intelligence capabilities, you’ve probably already upgraded.

macOS 27 Golden Gate Requirements

The Intel era has officially ended. macOS 27 Golden Gate runs exclusively on Macs with Apple silicon—no Intel-based Macs are supported. This completes the Apple silicon transition that began with the M1 chip in 2020 (see “ Apple M1 Chip Powers New MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and Mac mini,” 10 November 2020). If you’re still using an Intel-based Mac, macOS 26 Tahoe will continue to receive security updates for 2 years, meaning it will lose security viability in mid-2028.

macOS 27 will also be the last version of macOS to include the full Rosetta 2 translation environment. After macOS 27, Apple will retain only limited Rosetta functionality to support older games. If you rely on Intel-based apps, now is the time to find native Apple silicon alternatives.

House of the Dragon Season 3 Episode 5 places Alicent and Helaena inside one of the Red Keep’s hidden passages, where a planned escape quickly turns into a dangerous trap. Their disappearance adds fresh political tension while also showing how the castle’s secret tunnels can protect people, mislead them, or leave them buried beneath the seat of power.

The passage appears to connect with the maze built under the Red Keep during the reign of Maegor I Targaryen. Maegor ordered the construction of hidden doors, false walls, and escape routes so he could survive attacks or flee during a siege. He later killed the workers who knew the full design, which left the tunnels dangerous for anyone who entered without guidance.

Why Alicent and Helaena Become Trapped

Alicent and Helaena close the hidden door after entering the passage, then discover that someone has blocked the route ahead. Helaena drops their only light after a rat frightens her, leaving both women trapped in complete darkness with no clear way back.

The blocked path suggests that someone deliberately closed this escape route. Mysaria stands out as the main suspect because she appears to know what happens across the Red Keep, including private details about Helaena. Larys Strong also remains a possible suspect because he often plans and understands how people behave under pressure.

Their Disappearance Creates Political Trouble

Rhaenyra will probably assume that Alicent and Helaena escaped from the castle, while Mysaria can use that belief to increase suspicion inside the Black faction. Daemon may reach a different conclusion and suspect that Ormund Hightower arranged their removal as part of a wider Green plan.

Alicent and Helaena will likely escape the tunnels, but their temporary disappearance can still push both sides toward further conflict. The scene also gives the Red Keep a stronger role in the story, as its hidden structure becomes another source of fear, confusion, and political danger.
